name: Tagwana Senoufo
world_status: statement found in an open source

earlier_scan.source_named: Mensah, E.N.A. & Tchagbale, M. Zakari 1983, Atlas des langues gur de Cote d'Ivoire (cited on Glottolog tagw1240); covers Tagwana; not online

new_statements.quote: If some conditions are met, when two morphemes come together, the last vowel of the first morpheme or word deletes, and a coda is created. We refrain from calling the process “vowel syncope”, since that would imply that it is an unstressed vowel that is deleted. However, there is no evidence whatever for stress in Fròʔò. Vowel deletion in Fròʔò touches all vowels equally. [p. 2:] Fròʔò has three level tones, high (H), mid (M) and low (L). There are no contour tones. The syllable is the tone bearing unit (TBU) and every syllable in every word carries its own tone, regardless of the category and the length of the word.
new_statements.citation: Traoré, Yranahan & Caroline Féry. 2019. Syllable structure and loanword adaptation in Fròʔò. In S. Lotven, S. Bongiovanni, P. Weirich, R. Botne & S. G. Obeng (eds.), African linguistics across the disciplines: Selected papers from the 48th Annual Conference on African Linguistics, 1–28. Berlin: Language Science Press. DOI 10.5281/zenodo.3520565
new_statements.locator: p. 13, §3.1 'Vowel deletion leading to CVC syllables' (tone background p. 2)
new_statements.reading: no word stress according to the source
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (28 pp., text layer, LangSci open-access chapter, DOI 10.5281/zenodo.3520565). Printed p.13, §3.1 'Vowel deletion leading to CVC syllables' reads exactly: 'If some conditions are met, when two morphemes come together, the last vowel of the first morpheme or word deletes, and a coda is created. We refrain from calling the process “vowel syncope”, since that would imply that it is an unstressed vowel that is deleted. However, there is no evidence whatever for stress in Fròʔò. Vowel deletion in Fròʔò touches all vowels equally.[fn.5]' with fn.5 'High vowels are not deleted more easily than mid or low vowels, as is the case in the neighboring Bamana...'. The second (tone) part of the quo…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Fròʔò (Tagbana) is described as a three-level tone language in which every syllable bears its own tone; the authors (one a native-speaker linguist) state there is no evidence at all for word stress, and vowel deletion is not conditioned by any stressed/unstressed distinction.
new_statements.exceptions: None in this source. Note a later exploratory proposal by the same first author (Traore 2024, IJAMRS 4(1): 1053) that certain nouns carry an underlying lexical 'quantitative accent' manifesting as vowel lengthening before [l]; it gives no placement rule and does not claim general word stress.
new_statements.domain_note: Statement is about the word-level phonology of the Fròʔò dialect (Fronan); made in passing while motivating terminology for a vowel-deletion process, not in a dedicated prosody section. Tone (H/M/L + floating tones) is the described word-prosodic system (Rialland, Traoré & Féry 2021).
new_statements.identity_note: All opened sources describe the Fròʔò dialect of Tagbana, spoken around Fronan (the second author's native variety); Glottolog tagw1240 'Tagwana Senoufo' [tgw] covers Tagbana as a whole (other dialects: Takper of Niakaramandougou described by Hérault & Mlanhoro 1973, Katiola dialect in Bothel's mss.). No separate glottocode for Fròʔò is known to me.

sources.citation: Rialland, Annie, Yranahan Traoré & Caroline Féry. 2021. Nominal tonology and spreading rules in Tagbana (Fròʔò dialect). Studies in African Linguistics 50(2): 167–195. DOI 10.32473/sal.v50i2.117236
sources.note: Nothing on stress: three level tones (H, M, L) plus floating (H)/(L), syllable = TBU; recursive prosodic hierarchy (ω, Φ, ι) motivated by tone sandhi domains only; the foot appears only in the generic hierarchy diagram, no Tagbana foot/stress claim.

sources.citation: Traore, Yranahan. 2024. A morphophonological approach of vowels lengthening in Tagbana. International Journal of Advanced Multidisciplinary Research and Studies 4(1): 1046–1058. DOI 10.62225/2583049x.2024.4.1.2339
sources.note: p.1053 §2.3: as an exploratory alternative for why some nouns but not verbs lengthen a vowel before [l], proposes 'lengthening triggered by accent. Accent is not due to any morphological or phonological operation, rather it is an underlying and lexical property of the words themselves' (a quantitative accent); no placement rule, no general word-stress claim.

sources.citation: Traoré, Yranahan & Caroline Féry. 2018. Nominal classes and phonological agreement in Tagbana (Fròʔò). In R. Bennett et al. (eds.), Hana-bana: A Festschrift for Junko Ito and Armin Mester, 1–29. Santa Cruz: University of California. (author copy from caroline-fery.de)
sources.note: Nothing on stress; vowel/nasal harmony and alliterative concord. Only fn.9 (p.9) relays a reviewer's hypothesis that disyllabic class markers may involve 'a prosodic boundary (foot or prosodic word)', left unanswered.
